question_text: A program checks whether each of 100 000 usernames has already been taken. One version stores the taken usernames in a Python list and uses "name in taken_list"; another stores them in a Python set and uses "name in taken_set". Explain how the underlying mechanics of a Python set make the second version faster, and why Python allows strings, but not lists, to be elements of a set.
adaptation_rationale: Original question written by Claude (single-agent Chunk 3 continuation, 2026-11-04) for a syllabus statement with no linked question at handover; no historical source question or official marking status claimed.
solution: A list membership test compares the name with the elements one by one (linear search), which is O(n). A Python set is implemented as a hash table: the name is passed through a hash function that gives the index of the slot where it would be stored, so only that slot (and any colliding entries) needs to be checked, giving O(1) average-case lookup. The same hashing means a value already present is found when adding, so duplicates are not stored. Elements must be hashable, meaning their hash value must never change: strings are immutable, so their hash is fixed, but a list could be changed after insertion, which would change its hash and leave it in the wrong slot, so lists are not allowed.

marking_points.criterion: List membership is a linear search, O(n) comparisons.
A set uses a hash function to compute the storage location (hash table).
So lookup checks only that location/collisions, average O(1), independent of the number of usernames.
Elements must be hashable/immutable: a mutable list could change its hash after insertion and be stored in the wrong place; strings are immutable.

acceptable_alternatives: Accept reference to Java HashSet with equivalent mechanics. Accept "constant time on average" for O(1).
